opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most important things for us, and it's something we've been quite deliberate about from the beginning.

When you're building models, it's very easy to optimize for the things you can measure easily: academic benchmarks, leaderboards, that kind of thing. They're useful, but they don't always reflect what matters when someone deploys a model in production. Maybe a bank needs the model to follow a very specific output format reliably, or an industrial customer needs it to work well in a language or domain that's barely represented on the public web. You only learn those things by being close to the people who deploy the models every day.

So having the solutions team and the research team talk constantly means feedback comes back very fast. When the applied team sees the model failing in a particular way, maybe on function calling, long-context retrieval, or a certain kind of reasoning, that goes straight to the researchers, and it can shape what data we collect or what we prioritize in the next training run. It's not a ticket that sits in a queue for three months.

It goes the other way too. Researchers who see how the models are actually used tend to make better decisions. They get an intuition for what matters and what's just a nice number on a paper. And the solutions people get early access to new capabilities, so they can tell customers what's coming and help design the right systems around it.

At our size, we can't afford to have research disconnected from reality. We don't have infinite compute or infinite people, so we have to be quite focused, and the best way to stay focused is to stay close to real use cases. It's a big part of why we've been able to move fast and ship models that people actually find useful, rather than just models that look good on benchmarks.

r001.rationale: The response says the applied team reports ways the model fails in customer use, and that this feedback reaches researchers and can shape data collection or priorities for the next training run.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the things that actually makes Mistral work, and honestly, it's a big part of why we set the company up the way we did.

When I was at Meta working on LLaMA, the research was in some ways very far from the people who actually had to deploy things. You'd publish a paper, you'd release weights, and then you'd kind of hope that somebody somewhere found it useful. You didn't really get the feedback loop. And the feedback loop is where a lot of the interesting problems are.

So at Mistral we try to keep the distance between the people training the models and the people who are sitting with customers very short. And it matters in both directions. The solution teams see very concretely where the model fails. A customer in banking or in defense will tell you, "the model is great on this, but it hallucinates on this kind of document," or "it's too slow for our use case," or "we need it to run on this hardware." Those are not things you discover from academic benchmarks. If that signal goes straight back to the research team, you end up prioritizing very different things than if you just optimize MMLU or whatever the benchmark of the week is.

And in the other direction, the research team can tell the solution people what's actually possible. There's a lot of confusion in the market about what a model can do, what fine-tuning will fix, what needs more data, what's just a prompting issue. If the person in front of the customer can go ask the person who trained the model, you avoid promising things that won't work, and you also avoid being too conservative on things that would.

The other thing I'd say is that it's good for the researchers themselves. It's very easy, if you only do research, to work on problems that are intellectually interesting but that nobody actually needs. Seeing a real deployment, where someone is actually relying on the model, is a very good filter. It keeps you honest. Some of the best things we've shipped, like the work on small models that run efficiently, or the function-calling stuff, came more from "people keep asking for this" than from a grand research vision.

Of course there's a tension. Research needs some room to work on things that won't pay off for a year, and you don't want every researcher to be pulled into solving one customer's problem this week. So we do protect part of the team for longer-horizon work. But the default is that the two sides talk to each other constantly, they sit close to each other, and I think that's a real advantage for a company our size compared to the bigger labs.

r001.rationale: The response says customer failure reports reach researchers and change what they prioritize, but it does not clearly connect that feedback to improvements in the next model version.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very useful feedback loop. When you work on research, it’s easy to focus on benchmarks, but they don’t necessarily capture what people need when they actually use the models. The solution team sees where models work well, where they fail, and what customers are struggling with. Bringing that feedback directly to researchers helps us choose better problems to work on.

And it goes in both directions. Researchers can explain what’s becoming possible and help the solution team approach a problem differently. You want that exchange to be fast, rather than having research develop something in isolation and then hand it over. Ultimately, it helps us build better models and make them more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says customer struggles and model failures help researchers choose problems and build better models, but it does not connect that feedback to improvements in the next model version.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is having a very short feedback loop. The research team can build a model that looks very good on benchmarks, but when the solution team works with customers, they see where it actually struggles and what people need. That gives us a much better sense of which research problems to prioritize.

And it works in both directions. The solution team needs to understand what the models can do, what their limitations are, and what capabilities are coming. Keeping the teams close helps us turn research advances into something useful, and practical problems into research questions.

r001.rationale: The response says customer struggles can help prioritize research and turn practical problems into research questions, but it does not clearly connect that feedback to improvements in the next model version.
